courses.description:
This course is intended for students who need to acquire the knowledge and skills of one-variable calculus at a general level for the studies in mathematics, science, engineering and other areas. The course places special emphasis on conceptual understanding and computational techniques.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken MATH1018, IMSC2018, 2028, 2058, 2068, 2230 or students who are taking MATH1520 in the same term.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking this course, students are expected to be able to:
• Define and distinguish the usual concepts used in one variable calculus
• Logically prove basic statements in one variable calculus
• Calculate various differential quantities and solve problems using one variable calculus
• Apply the methods of one variable calculus to standard problems in physics, engineering, or business economics
• Appreciate the rationale and impact of one variable calculus to human development in science and technology.

courses.description:
This course is designed as a continuation of the HKDSE Mathematics (Compulsory Part) or equivalent, to familiarize mathematics major students with elementary and foundational algebraic and geometric methods which will help the study of other MATH courses.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken MATH1028, 1050/1058 or students who are taking MATH1525 in the same term. Co-requisite: MATH1010/1018.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students are able to:

* Understand the content of simple mathematical statements.
* Apply various results about elementary algebraic methods and geometric methods in simple computational type problems.
* Deduce, with reference of definitions, (but if relevant and necessary, with various established classical results assumed) simple mathematical results in elementary algebra, such as divisibility (for integers), inequalities (about real numbers), complex numbers, polynomials and their roots.
* Read off and describe solutions of simple equations and inequalities through the use of algebraic methods, and/or graphical methods.
* Handle simple geometric problems with algebraic methods, and visualize simple algebraic problems through geometry.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Honours Essential Mathematical Methods

This course is designed as a continuation of the HKDSE Mathematics (Compulsory Part) or equivalent, to familiarize mathematics major students with foundational algebraic and geometric methods which will help in the study of other MATH courses (including Honours courses).
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.

courses.learning_outcomes:

* Apply various results about elementary algebraic methods and geometric methods in computational type problems.
* Deduce, with reference of definitions, (but if relevant and necessary, with various established classical results assumed) mathematical results in elementary algebra, such as divisibility (for integers), inequalities (about real numbers), complex numbers, polynomials and their roots.
* Read off and describe solutions of simple equations and inequalities through the use of algebraic methods, and/or graphical methods.
* Handle simple geometric problems with algebraic methods, and visualize simple algebraic problems through geometry.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Linear Algebra I
courses.description:
This course is intended for students who need to acquire the knowledge and skills of linear algebra. The course emphasizes the fundamental principles, reasoning of mathematics and also applications, but generality instead of particular usage will be the focus.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken MATH1038,1630, IMSC1038, 2048, 2078 or students who are taking MATH1550 in the same term.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Students are able to
- define and distinguish the usual concepts used in linear algebra
- logically prove basic statements in linear algebra
- solve problems using linear algebra, including those in an abstract setting
- apply the methods of linear algebra to standard problems in physics, engineering, or business economics
- appreciate the rationale and impact of linear algebra to human development in science and technology

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Honours Linear Algebra I
courses.description:
This course is intended as the first course on linear algebra for MATH major students. The course emphasizes the fundamental concepts and principles in linear algebra, and focuses on rigorous reasoning of mathematical statements, computational techniques as well as applications.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken MATH1030,1630,IMSC1038,2048,2078 or students who are taking MATH1550 in the same term. Pre-requisite: [Alternative 1] Grade B or above in each of MATH1018, 1028. [Alternative 2] Grade A- or above in each of MATH1010, 1025.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Students are able to
- define and distinguish the usual concepts used in linear algebra
- logically prove basic statements in linear algebra and understand ideas behind the proofs of theorems
- solve problems using linear algebra, including those in an abstract setting
- apply the methods of linear algebra to standard problems in physics, engineering, or business economics
- appreciate the rationale and impact of linear algebra to human development in science and technology

courses.learning_outcomes:
Students are able to
- Define and distinguish the usual concepts used in calculus
- Calculate differential and integral quantities in one variable calculus
- Apply calculus to solve problems in science, technology and other areas
- Appreciate the rationale and use of one variable calculus in the development of science, technology and other areas

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Basic Mathematics for Science and Technology
courses.description: This course is designed as a continuation of the HKDSE Mathematics (Compulsory Part) or equivalent, to give students who intend to study general science subjects a solid foundation for the use of basic mathematics in various disciplines in physical science, life science and statistics, and for the study of the applications of calculus and linear algebra in science and technology.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken any one of MATH1010/1018, 1025/1028, 1530, 1610, 1620.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students are able to:

* recognize and handle elementary mathematical entities appearing in physical science, life science and statistics.
* apply elementary algebraic and graphical methods in modelling and/or solving problems in physical science, life science, and statistics.
* manipulate with algebraic entities and simple inequalities logically.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Basic Mathematics for Business and Social Sciences

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 407

courses.description: This course equips students with the necessary basic mathematics for applications in business and social sciences. It is particularly suitable for those without much mathematics training in high school. Concepts will be introduced by examples in these disciplines.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken any one of MATH1010/1018, 1025/1028, 1030/1038, 1525, 1610, 1620 2xxx or above.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students are able to:

* Demonstrate mathematical skills beyond school level.
* Apply elementary mathematics to solve simple problems in business and social sciences.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Intermediate Mathematics for Business and Social Sciences
courses.description: This course is a continuation of MATH1530, with emphasis on the use of one-variable calculus and elementary linear algebra in the study of business and social sciences. Topics include: limits of sequences, continuous functions, differential and integral calculus of one real variable, first-order differential equations, basic numerical methods, vectors and matrices, determinants, systems of linear equations.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken MATH1010/1018. Pre-requisite: MATH1530.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students are able to:---

* Demonstrate conceptual understanding in basic and classical results in limits of sequences, continuous functions, differential and integral calculus, numerical methods, first-order differential equations, and elementary linear algebra.
* Demonstrate computational skills in differential and integral calculus, numerical methods, first-order differential equations, and elementary linear algebra.
* Apply basic and classical results about limits of sequences, continuous functions, differential and integral calculus, numerical methods, first-order differential equations, vectors, matrices, determinants, and system of linear equations in solving simple problems concerned with business, finance and social sciences.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: University Mathematics for Financial Studies
courses.description: This course is designed for students who wish to specialize in mathematics related financial studies. It is suitable for those who have mathematical background in one-variable calculus, at the level of MATH1535 or MATH1010, and in elementary linear algebra, at the level of MATH1535 or HKDSE Mathematics Extended Module II. It is the purpose of this course to enable students to make a smooth transition into the study of essential mathematical tools in finance, especially multivariable calculus and linear algebra.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Pre-requisite: MATH1010 or 1535.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students are able to:

* Demonstrate conceptual understanding in basic and classical results in, multivariable differential and integral calculus, and linear algebra.
* Demonstrate computational skills in multivariable differential and integral calculus, and linear algebra.
* Apply basic and classical results about multivariable differential and integral calculus, and linear algebra, in solving simple problems concerned with business, finance and social sciences.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Methods of Matrices and Linear Algebra

William M W Mong Eng Bldg 404

courses.description: This course is intended as an introduction to elementary linear algebra through a matrix oriented approach. Its content emphasizes on the methods and techniques for the acquisition of basic understanding and calculation skills in various elementary topics in linear algebra (such as matrix operations, systems of linear equations, determinants, orthogonality, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, linear transformations). The course is suitable for students without much mathematics background and intended to be major in Statistics, Economics, Business, Life Sciences and Social Sciences.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken MATH1030/1038, 1610, 1630.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Linear Algebra for Advanced Accounting Analytics
courses.description: This course is intended as a non-technical introduction to the use of linear algebra in business, economics, finance, and accounting. Its content emphasizes on intuitive understanding of concepts and methods in linear algebra, and their applications in various branches of modern technology relevant to business, economics, finance, and accounting.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken any one of MATH1010/1018, 1025/1028, 1030/1038, 1510, 1520, 1525, 1530, 1550, 1630, 2xxx or above.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students are able to:

* Understand the basic terminologies and notations in linear algebra.
* Perform simple manipulations concerned with matrix, vector, determinant, inner product and norm.
* Identify, in concrete situations, properties and constructions associated with individual matrices and vectors, or collections of matrices and vectors.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Calculus for Advanced Accounting Analytics
courses.description: This course is intended as a non-technical introduction to the use of calculus of one and several variables in business, economics, finance, and accounting. Its content emphasizes on intuitive understanding of concepts and methods in calculus, and their applications in various branches of modern technology relevant to business, economics, finance, and accounting.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken any one of MATH1010/1018, 1025/1028, 1030/1038, 1510, 1520, 1525, 1530, 1550, 1630, 2xxx or above.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students are able to:

* Understand the basic terminologies and notations in calculus of one and several variables.
* Perform simple manipulations concerned with limit, derivative, partial derivative, integral and double integral.
* Identify, in concrete situations, properties and constructions associated with limit, derivative, partial derivative, integral and double integral.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Linear Algebra and Applications
courses.description: This course is intended to introduce the methods and concepts in linear algebra and matrix theory which are often used in the studies of physical and biological sciences, data science and machine learning, business, accounting and finance. Topics are selected from: systems of linear equations, matrix algebra, vector spaces, linear transformation, determinants, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, inner product, special matrices and matrix factorizations.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken MATH1030/1038. Pre-requisite: MATH1010/1018 or 1510 or 1520 or ENGG1120/ESTR1005 or (ECON1101 and ECON1111).
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students are able to:

* demonstrate understanding of basic properties of key concepts and tools in elementary linear algebra, such as systems of linear equations, matrix algebra, vector spaces, linear transformations, determinants, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, inner product, special matrices and matrix factorizations.
* demonstrate understanding on how to apply the aforementioned tools in studying and/or solving problems in linear algebra which originate from physical and biological sciences, data science and machine learning, business, accounting and finance.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Advanced Calculus I
courses.description:
This course is intended to introduce the basics of the calculus of functions of several variables. Topics include: vectors, geometry of Euclidean spaces, curves, limits, partial derivatives, differentiability, chain rule, first and second derivative test, maximum and minimum, Taylor polynomials, Lagrange multipliers, implicit function theorem.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who took MATH2018/2020/2028,IMSC2018,2028,2058,2068,2230 or taking MATH2530 in same term. Pre-requisite: [Option 1] MATH1010/1018. Check dept website for more options. Co-requisite MATH1030/1038/1050/1058/1090/1098/1630.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students understand the basic concepts and applications of the calculus of functions of several variables, including vectors, functions of several variables, partial derivatives and their applications, and extremum problems.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Honours Advanced Calculus I
courses.description:
This course is intended to introduce the basics of the calculus of functions of several variables. Topics include: vectors, geometry of Euclidean spaces, curves, limits, partial derivatives, differentiability, chain rule, first and second derivative test, maximum and minimum, Taylor polynomials, Lagrange multipliers, implicit function theorem.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students taken MATH2010/2020/2028,IMSC or concurrently taking MATH2530. Pre-requisite: [Option 1] Grade B- or above in two of MATH1018, 1028, 1038. [Option 2] Grade A- or above in two of MATH1010, 1025, 1030. Co-requisite MATH1050/1058/1090/1098.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students understand the basic concepts and applications of the calculus of functions of several variables, including vectors, functions of several variables, partial derivatives and their applications, and extremum problems, as well as the ideas behind the proofs of the theorems.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Advanced Calculus II
courses.description:
This is a continuation of MATH2010. The following topics will be discussed: multiple integrals: double integrals, areas, volumes, surface areas, change of variables; vector analysis: line integrals, surface integrals, Green theorem, divergence theorem, Stokes theorem.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for students taken MATH2028, IMSC2018/2028/2058/2068/2230 or students taking MATH2550 in same term.
Pre-requisite: [Alternative 1] MATH2010/2018. [Alternative 2] Grade A- or above in two of ENGG1125/ESTR1007, ENGG1120/ESTR1005, ENGG1130/ESTR1006.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students understand the theory and the applications of multiple integrals. These include line integrals, multiple integrals, surface integrals and applications to vector analysis.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Honours Advanced Calculus II
courses.description:
This is a continuation of MATH2018. The following topics will be discussed: multiple integrals in n-dimensions: areas and n-volumes, surface areas, volumes of submanifolds and hypersurfaces in n-space, change of variables; vector analysis: line integrals, surface integrals, integration on submanifolds, Green theorem, divergence theorem and Stokes theorem in n-dimensions.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students taken MATH2020,IMSC2018/2028/2058/2068/2230 or taking MATH2550 in same term. Pre-requisite [Option 1] Grade B- or above in MATH2018 and one of MATH1058, 1098, 2048. [Option 2] Grade A- or above in MATH2010 and one of MATH1050, 1090, 2040
courses.learning_outcomes: Students understand the theory and the applications of multiple integrals. These include line integrals, multiple integrals, surface integrals and applications to vector analysis, as well as the ideas behind the proofs of the theorems.

Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken MATH2048, IMSC1038/2048/2078. Pre-requisite: (MATH1030/1038 or 1630 or ENGG1120/ESTR1005) and (MATH1050/1058 or 1090/1098).

Students are expected to understand the ideas underlying the concepts and write mathematical proofs.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Advanced Linear Algebra
courses.description: This is a course on advanced topics in linear algebra, with emphasis on the study of vector spaces from an abstract, coordinate-free point of view, and on the proving of generalizations of results covered in an elementary linear algebra course. Topics include: abstract vector spaces, linear transformations, matrix representation, nullity and rank, properties of determinants, diagonalization, Cayley-Hamilton theorem, inner product spaces, normal and self-adjoint operators, unitary and orthogonal operators, bilinear forms, dual spaces, canonical forms, spectral theorem.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken any one of MATH1025/1028, 1090/1098, 2040/2048.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students are able to understand:

* more advanced topics in linear algebra: abstract vector spaces and linear transformations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, canonical forms of matrices and linear transformations, inner product spaces, duals spaces and bilinear forms, spectral theorems.
* the ideas underlying the concepts and write rigorous mathematical proofs.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Honours Linear Algebra II
courses.description:
This is a continuation of MATH1038. Topics include: abstract vector spaces, linear transformations, matrix representation, nullity and rank, properties of determinants, diagonalization, Cayley-Hamilton theorem, inner product spaces, normal and self-adjoint operators, unitary and orthogonal operators, bilinear forms, dual spaces, canonical forms, spectral theorem.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for students taken MATH2040,IMSC1038/2048/2078. 
Pre-requisite:[Option 1] Grade B- or above in one of (MATH1038,2018) & Grade B- or above in one of MATH1058,1098. [Option 2] Grade A- or above in MATH1030 & Grade A- or above in one of MATH1050,1090.
courses.learning_outcomes: We expect students to understand more advanced topics in linear algebra: abstract vector spaces and linear transformations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, canonical forms of matrices and linear transformations, inner product spaces, duals spaces and bilinear forms, spectral theorems. Students are expected to understand the ideas underlying the concepts and write rigorous mathematical proofs.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Mathematical Analysis I
courses.description:
This course is intended to provide conceptual understanding in the theory of functions of one real variable. Topics include: real numbers, real valued functions, set notations; limits of sequences, convergence, Bolzano-Weierstrass; limits of functions, continuous functions, uniform continuity.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken MATH2058, IMSC2018/2028/2058/2068/2230. Pre-requisite: [Option 1] [MATH1010/1018 (or Grade B or above in MATH1510/1520)], and (MATH1050/1058/1090/1098). Check dept website for more options.
courses.learning_outcomes:
We emphasize the rigorous epsilon-delta approach to analysis, which is crucial for a solid study of analysis. After taking and passing this course, a student is expected
- to understand the axioms of the real number system (constructions such as the Dedekind cuts are not necessary),
- to know the basic properties of countable and uncountable sets (must know that real numbers and irrational numbers are uncountable) and the statement of the continuum hypothesis,
- to familiarize with the concept of limits of sequences and functions, and
- to know the concept of continuity and uniform continuity for functions on the real line as well as relevant results

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Honours Mathematical Analysis I
courses.description:
This course is intended to provide conceptual understanding in the theory of functions of one or more real variables. Topics include: real numbers, real valued functions, set notations; limits of sequences (including limsup and liminf), convergence, Bolzano-Weierstrass, infinite series; limits of functions, continuous functions, uniform continuity.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for students taken MATH2050,IMSC2018/2028/2058/2068/2230.
Pre-requisite: [Option 1] Grade B- or above in each of MATH1018,1028,1098 OR in each of MATH1058 & 2018 [Option 2] Grade A- or above in each of MATH1010,1025,1090 OR in each of MATH1050 & 2010
courses.learning_outcomes:
We emphasize the rigorous epsilon-delta approach to analysis, which is crucial for a solid study of analysis. After taking and passing this course, a student is expected
- to understand the axioms of the real number system (constructions such as the Dedekind cuts are not necessary),
- to know the basic properties of countable and uncountable sets (must know that real numbers and irrational numbers are uncountable) and the statement of the continuum hypothesis,
- to familiarize with the concept of limits of sequences, series and functions, and
- to know the concept of continuity and uniform continuity for functions on the real line, on higher dimensional Euclidean spaces, as well as relevant results.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Mathematical Analysis II
courses.description:
This is a continuation of MATH2050. Topics include: differentiability, mean-value theorem, Taylor theorem, convexity; integrability, fundamental theorem of calculus, improper integrals; power series, radius of convergence, series for elementary functions; infinite series, convergence and divergence, rearrangement; sequence and series of functions.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken MATH2068, IMSC2018/2028/2058/2068/2230. Pre-requisite: MATH2050/2058.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking and passing this course a student will be able
(1) to know the properties of differentiable functions and convex functions,
(2) to use Darboux sums to study Riemann integrable functions and learn the Taylor formula with remainder,
(3) to understand the fundamental theorems of calculus which relate integration to differentiation, and
(4) to know basic tests for convergence of infinite series and functions, and
(5) to know how the elementary functions including the exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions are rigorously defined.
In (1)-(3) he/she should master those examples and counterexamples which illustrate the applicability of various theorems.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Introductory Real Analysis
courses.description: This is a course on the theory of differential and integral calculus of one or several real variables. It is based on rigorous theory and state-of-the-art methodology. Topics include: differentiability in one or higher dimensions, mean-value theorem, Taylor theorem, convexity; integrability in one or higher dimensions, fundamental theorem of calculus, improper integrals, Fubini’s theorem for double series and continuous functions; power series, radius of convergence, series for elementary functions, real analyticity; sequence and series of functions, uniform convergence.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken any one of MATH1025/1028, 1090/1098, 2060/2068.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students are able to:

1. demonstrate understanding on the properties of differentiable functions and convex functions, for one or several real variables,
2. demonstrate understanding on the properties of Riemann integrable functions, for one or several real variables,
3. demonstrate understanding on the fundamental theorems of calculus,
4. demonstrate understanding on the basic theory of convergence for infinite series of functions (including power series),
5. demonstrate understanding on how the elementary functions (including the exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions) are rigorously defined.

In 1, 2, 4 he/she are expected to be able to demonstrate understanding on those examples and counterexamples which illustrate the applicability of various theorems.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Honours Mathematical Analysis II
courses.description:
This is a continuation of MATH2058. Topics include: differentiability in one or higher dimensions, mean-value theorem, Taylor theorem, convexity; integrability in one or higher dimensions, fundamental theorem of calculus, improper integrals, Fubini’s theorem for double series and continuous functions; power series, radius of convergence, series for elementary functions, real analyticity; sequence and series of functions, uniform convergence.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.

(c) perform tasks involving modeling, simulation, data analysis, and visualization

courses.description:
This course is to introduce the basic properties of complex functions and analytic functions and to illustrate the important use of these theories to other branches of mathematics and sciences. Topics include: complex numbers; limits, continuity and derivatives, Cauchy-Riemann equations, analytic functions; elementary functions; mapping by elementary functions; Contours integrals, Cauchy-Goursat theorem, Cauchy integral formula, Morera’s theorem, maximum moduli of functions, the fundamental theorem of algebra; Taylor series and Laurent’s series; residues and poles, evaluation of infinite real integrals.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.

courses.learning_outcomes:
Students are able to:
1. Define and recognize complex differentiable functions and analytic functions.
2. State the basic properties of analytic functions and major theories about these functions related to contour integration.
3. Work out the local properties at zeros or singularities of analytic functions by series or integrals.
4. Apply residue theory to evaluate real integrals.

courses.description:
This course is a continuation of MATH2060. It provides rigorous treatment on further topics in mathematical analysis. This course is essential for studying advanced mathematics, pure or applied, to the level beyond undergraduate. Topics include: Fourier series, pointwise and uniform convergence of Fourier series, $L^2$-completeness of Fourier series. Parseval's identity; metric spaces, open sets and continuity, completion of a metric space, contraction mapping principle; the space of continuous functions, Weierstrass approximation theorem, Stone-Weierstrass theorem, Baire category theorem, continuous but nowhere differentiable functions, equicontinuity and Ascoli's theorem; implicit and inverse function theorems, functional dependence and independence; fundamental existence and uniqueness theorem for differential equations, the continuous dependence of the solution on initial time and values.

Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken any one of IMSC2018, 2028, 2058, 2068, 2230. Pre-requisite: MATH2060 or 2068.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking this course, a student will be able to
1. how to expand a function into a Fourier series and under what conditions the Fourier series converges to the function,
2. describe to describe limit and continuity in terms of open sets in a metric space,
3. use the contraction principle to solve some equations,
4. apply the fundamental results such as Stone-Weierstrass theorem, Baire category theorem and Ascoli's theorem in his/her further studies in analysis,
5. understand the proofs of the implicit and inverse function theorem and many of their applications, and
6. the details in the proof of the fundamental existence and uniqueness of differential equations, a theorem stated in MATH3270.

Fundamental Group: loop, space of loops, homotopy, calculation of fundamental groups of some spaces, path lifting lemma, homotopy lifting lemma, fundamental groups of quotient spaces of free discrete group actions.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Number Theory

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 803

courses.description:
This course is intended to introduce the students to the intriguing structure of integers. Topics are usually selected from: divisibility theory of the integers, primes, congruence, Fermat's little theorem, some arithmetic functions, primitive roots and indices. Students are expected to have knowledge in MATH2070/2078, or equivalent.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.learning_outcomes:
- Students learn basic concepts and results about divisibility of integers, including greatest common divisor, Euclid’s algorithm, fundamental theorem of arithmetic, properties of primes.
- Students learn some typical arithmetic functions and learn the Mobius inversion formulae, learn some properties of the Riemann zeta-function.
- Students learn some fundamental results about congruence, such as Chinese remainder theorem, Fermat, Euler, Lagrange’s theorems; and learn how to solve linear congruence equations; learn the concepts and properties of primitive roots and indices.
- Students learn some concepts and results about quadratic residues, such as Legendre symbol, Jacobi’s symbol and law of quadratic reciprocity; learn how to solve quadratic congruence equations.
- Students learn some elementary results on quadratic forms: the representations of integers by binary forms, in particular the representation of integers as the sum of squares.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Operations Research
courses.description:
Operations Research (OR) refers to the science of decision making. It uses various problem-solving techniques and methods to analyse system behavior and improve decision-making and efficiency by arriving at optimal or near optimal solutions to complex decision problems. This course provides a fundamental account of the basic results and techniques of Linear Programming (LP), network optimization and integer programming in Operations Research. There is an equal emphasis on all three aspects of theory, algorithms as well as applications, which provides essential optimization concept and background for more advanced studies in Operations Research. Students taking this course are expected to have basic knowledge in linear algebra. They are also expected to have basic programming skills in some programming language (such as MATLAB, C++, Python).
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Pre-requisite: MATH1030/1038 or 1630 or ENGG1120/ESTR1005.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Numerical Analysis
courses.description:
Floating-point numbers and roundoff errors, absolute and relative errors, stable and unstable computations, solutions of nonlinear equations, linear systems, interpolation, numerical differentiation, and numerical integration. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in advanced calculus and linear algebra. They are also expected to have basic programming skills in some programming language (such as MATLAB, C++, Python).
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Students are expected to understand the fundamental concepts involved in numerical analysis, and learn some basic approaches and techniques in solving linear and nonlinear systems, constructing interpolations and do numerical differntiation and integration. The basic learning outcomes include:

- Students understand the basic concepts in scientific computings, including fixed-point numbers, floating-point numbers, single and double precision, overflow and underflow, roundoff errors, absolute and relative errors, stable and unstable computations.

- Students learn some basic knowledge in floating-point arithmetic and know how to use the backward error analysis to estimate possible errors generated in numerical computings.

- Students learn some basic concepts in solving nonlinear equations of one variable: iterative methods, rate of convergence, local and global convergence; learn some classical methods for solving nonlinear equations of one variable: bisection methods, Newton's method, quasi-Newton's method and fixed-point iteration, and learn how to analyse convergence of these method.

- Students learn some basic methods for solving linear system of equations: Cholesky factorization, LU and LDU factorization, forward- and backward-substitutions for traingular systems, Gaussian elimination.

- Students learn sensitivity analysis of the solutions of linear systems with respect to some errors in their coefficient matrices or in their right-hand sides, and understand condition numbers and their importance.

- Students learn three polynomial interpolations, Newton form of interpolations, Lagrange and spline interpolations, and learn how to estimate the interpolation errors.

- Students learn some popular numerical integrations: trapezoidal and composite trapezoidal rules, Simpson and composite Simpson rules, Newton-Cotes quadrature rule, Gaussian quadrature rules, and learn how to estimate the errors of quadrature rules.

- Students learn some basic numerical differentiation techniques: forward differences, backward differences, central differences, and understand how to estimate the errors of these difference schemes.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Numerical Methods for Differential Equations

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 803
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 803
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 803
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 803

courses.description:
Numerical solution of ordinary differential equations, numerical solution of partial differential equations. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in advanced calculus and linear algebra. They are also expected to have basic programming skills in some programming language (such as MATLAB, C++, Python).
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Students are expected to understand some fundamental concepts involved in numerical methods for differential equations, and learn some basic approaches and techniques in solving ordinary and partial differential equations. The basic learning outcomes include:

- Students understand the importance of differential equations in modeling real-world phenomena and understand the meanings and importance of numerical methods in solving general ordinary and partial differential equations.

- Students learn some basic mathematical method of verifying the well-posedness of a ordinary differential equation (ODE).

- For a given first order ODE, students learn how to construct Taylor-series methods and Runge-Kutta methods with orders up to four.

- Students learn some basic approaches to constructing multistep methods: the quadrature rule approach, test function approach by polynomials, Adams-Bashforth and Adams-Mouton methods. And learn how to solve ODEs using multistep methods and predictor-corrector methods.

- Students learn how to compute the orders of multistep methods, and how to analyse consistency, stability and convergence of multistep methods and understand the relationship between these three concepts.

- Students learn how to convert a higher order ODE into a system of first order ODEs and how to construct Taylor-series methods and Runge-Kutta methods for the resulting ODE system.

- Students learn some important numerical methods for solving stiff ODEs, and understand the importance of A-stability, absolute stability and regions of absolute stability.

- Students learn how to use the shooting method to transform a two-point boundary value problem into an initial value problem.

- Students learn some basic finite difference schemes and collocation methods to solve two-point boundary value problems.

- Students learn some basic finite difference schemes to solve the one- and two-dimensional parabolic equations, and know how to analyse the consistency, stability and convergence of a finite difference scheme.

- Students learn some simple finite element methods to solve the one- and two-dimensional parabolic equations.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Graph Theory
courses.description:
Definitions and applications of graphs and digraphs, Eulerian graphs, Hamiltonian graphs, path algorithm, connectivity, trees, planarity and coloring graphs. Students are expected to have knowledge in basic linear algebra (such as power of matrix, similar matrices, eigenvalues).
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Pre-requisite: MATH1030/1038 or 1550 or 1610 or 1630 or ENGG1120/ESTR1005.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students are expected to learn and appreciate the rigorous and theoretical foundations as well as to recognize important applications of Graph Theory. The ability to formulate a problem and develop a mathematical treatment is also enhanced.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Ordinary Differential Equations
courses.description:
Ordinary differential equations arise from quantitative description of natural and social phenomena. Topics are: method of explicit solution, linear equations and systems, series solutions, Sturm-Liouville boundary value problems, dynamical systems and stability, applications to mechanics, electrical networks and population of species.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Pre-requisite: MATH1030/1038 or 1630 or ENGG1120/ESTR1005.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking and passing this course, a student should be able
- to solve first or second order ODE’s by elementary methods such as change of variables and power series expansion,
- to understand the structure theory of linear systems of equations,
- on the theoretical side, to master the proof of the fundamental theorem on existence and uniqueness of solution to a general ODE, and
- to understand the basic concept of stability of a solution including some examples arising from mathematical biology.
- to know the set-up of the Sturm-Liouville boundary value problems.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Introductory Probability
courses.description:
Axioms of probability, conditional probability, independence, discrete random variables, continuous random variables, mean, variance and covariance, moment generating function, Poisson distributions, normal distributions, central limit theorem, law of large numbers, random walks, transition probabilities and Markov chains. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in advanced calculus.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken MIEG2440/ESTR2362.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students learn the basic concepts of probability. They include: conditional probability, random variables, distributions, expectation and Limit theorems. Also students learn their applications in physical science and engineering.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Mathematical Modeling
courses.description:
This course introduces the concept of mathematical modeling. Topics include: different modeling techniques such as modeling with differential equations and modeling with linear programming, forecasting; economic models such as Markov models, network models and financial models such as input-output models and scheduling models.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Students are expected to learn some basic techniques and mathematical tools to set up a mathematical model for a given real-world problem, and to be able to do simulations using a model and to know how to improve a model. The basic learning outcomes include:

- Students understand practical meanings and importance of mathematical modeling in various applications.

- For a given real-world process, students learn how to identify the problem to be modeled by selecting only those most important and relevant factors.

- For a given real-world process, students understand the basic procedures to set up a mathematical model.

- Students learn modeling with discrete dynamical systems and difference equations to predict the future based on what is known at the present and the observed changes.

- Students understand the concepts of long-time behaviors of solutions to a discrete dynamical system and their relation to equilibrium values of the system, and understand how to identify stability and instability of an equilibrium value.

- Students learn how to analyses the sensitivity of a model to its initial conditions and model parameters.

- For a given set of observed data, students learn how to formulate a model using the Chebyshev approximation criterion, the criterion of minimizing the sum of absolute deviations and the least-squares criterion. And understand the relations between the three criteria and learn some basic solution techniques to solve the resulting model systems.

- For a given real-world process, students learn how to find an appropriate model after trying various types of model functions.

- Students understand the advantages and disadvantages of polynomial models, and understand the smoothing effects by low-order polynomials.

- Students learn how to simulate deterministic behaviors by Monte Carlo algorithms and probabilistic behaviors by probability models.

- Students learn how to set up a discrete optimization model and solve linear programming models by simplex method.

- Students learn modeling with differential equations, and know how to plot phase lines and sketch solution curves based on equilibrium solutions and signs of first and second derivatives.

- Students learn how to apply the Lagrange multiplier method to solve constrained optimization problems.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Computational and Applied Mathematics
courses.description:
This course introduces the general solution methods used in computational and applied mathematics. The central topics are differential equations and matrix equations. Methods include Fourier series, orthogonal expansion, conformal mapping, Fourier integrals, complex integration, LU decomposition, Newton method, semi-direct and iterative methods, the finite element methods and fast Fourier transform. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in advanced calculus and linear algebra.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Students are expected to learn some general mathematical methods which are frequently used in computational and applied mathematics, as well as in the physics and engineering applications. The basic learning outcomes include:

- Students learn some basic techniques of solving two-point elliptic boundary value problems (BVPs), and understand how to formulate a BVP into an equivalent minimization problem and an equivalent variational problem.

- Students learn some basic vector calculus in Euclidiean space, including gradient, divergence and vorticity operations, and know how to express a differential equation in the rectangular coordinate system, cylindrical coordinate system and spherical coordinate system.

- Students learn how to compute a real and complex Fourier series for a given periodic function, and understand the relation between the real and complex Fourier series.

- Students learn how to solve some standard differential equations in certain nice domains, like Laplace equation in a unit disk, by using the Fourier series.

- Students learn how to construct a series of orthonormal polynomial functions by Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process.

- Students learn how to find the Fourier and inverse Fourier transforms, as well as the discrete Fourier transform for a given function.

- Students learn the LU factorization for a given matrix and its relation with Gaussian elimination.

- Students learn how to solve nonlinear systems of equations by Newton's method, and how to solve linear systems of equations by Jacobi, Gauss-Seidal and successive overrelaxation methods, and understand why these methods work or do not work for some linear or nonlinear systems.

- Students learn how to find the eigenvalues of a matrix by QR factorization and understand the mathematics behind.

- Students learn the fast Fourier transform and its applications.

- Students learn how to solve a two-point boundary value problem by a simple finite element method.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Foundation of Data Analytics
courses.description:
This course gives an introduction to computational data analytics, with emphasis on its mathematical foundations. The goal is to carefully develop and explore mathematical theories and methods that make up the backbone of modern mathematical data sciences, such as knowledge discovery in databases, machine learning, and mathematical artificial intelligence. Topics include mathematical foundations of probability, linear approximation and its polynomial and high dimensional extensions, proper orthogonal decomposition methods, optimization, theories of nonlinear neural network and approximations. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge of basic linear algebra. They are also expected to have basic programming skills in some programming language (such as MATLAB, C++, Python).
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Learning outcomes:
On completion of this course, students will be able to:
• Understand in-depth the various topics in modern data analysis and the technical difficulties in solving them
• Acquire knowledge about the foundation of computational data analytics
• Learn how to use various mathematical models to extract important information from big data
• Systematically evaluate the performance of different models to solve various data analysis problems
• Understand the importance of computational data analytics for real-world problems

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Big Data Computing
courses.description:
This course provides students with practical experience in using mathematical techniques for big data computing, numerical optimization and simulations of practical mathematical models through various programming and software implementation. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in mathematical foundation of data analytics.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Pre-requisite: AIST1110 or CSCI 1020 or CSCI1110 or CSCI1120 or CSCI1130 or CSCI1510 or CSCI1520 or CSCI1530 or CSCI1540 or ESTR1100 or ESTR1102 or IERG1080 or MATH2221.
courses.learning_outcomes:
On completion of this course, students will be able to:
• Acquire practical experiences in big data computing
• Use of common software packages for big data computing
• Learn how to use mathematical machine learning algorithms to solve problems
• Design solution strategies using sophisticated mathematical modelling and computational techniques for real life applications

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Mathematics of Machine Learning

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 407
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 407
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 407
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 407

courses.description: This course presents the fundamental mathematical theory for modern machine learning techniques, including empirical risk minimization (error decomposition, Rademacher complexity, covering number), optimization method (gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent), kernel methods, and deep neural networks (approximation theory and over-parameterization). Students are expected to have knowledge in MATH2040/2048, MATH2050/2058 and MATH2060/2068, or equivalent. Familiarity with basic concepts about probability theory (e.g., knowledge in MATH3280), and basic programming skills in some programming language (such as MATLAB, C++, Python) will be helpful though not compulsory.
courses.learning_outcomes: On completion of this course, students are able to understand some classical analysis techniques in statistical learning theory, and to familiarize the skills in learning theory.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Functional Analysis
courses.description:
Metric spaces, fixed point theorems, Banach spaces, Hilbert spaces, continuous linear operator, the Hahn-Banach extension theorem, the uniform boundedness principle and the open mapping theorem, and applications of the above topics. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in elementary analysis and linear algebra.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for students who have taken any one of IMSC2058, 2068, 2230.
Pre-requisite: 
[Alternative 1] MATH3060
[Alternative 2] Grade B- or above in both MATH2050/2058 and MATH2060/2068.
courses.learning_outcomes:
This is an advanced undergraduate course. We expect students to understand how linear algebra and analysis can be put together to become one of the most important fields of mathematics; we also emphasize the generality and depth of this treatment as a useful tool in many other disciplines and for graduate study.
- Students are expected to know the distance concept in metric spaces, and point set topology such as open sets and close sets, convergence, Cauchy sequences, completion, continuity.
- Students learn the concept of norm linear spaces, Banach spaces, compactness of finite dimensional spaces, bounded linear operators, functionals and dual spaces.
- Students learn inner product spaces, Hilbert spaces, orthogonality and direct sums. These concepts will be used in Fourier series and other classical orthogonal series.
- Students learn the Reiesz representation theorem on Hilbert space and use it to define the adjoint operators. An elementary theory on self-adjoint operator will be developed.
- Students learn the fundamental theorems for normed linear spaces: the Hahn-Banach theorem and its applications to the Reiesz representation theorem on continuous function space, the uniform boundedness principle, the open mapping theorem. The concept of strong and weak convergence will be introduced.
- Students learn how to solve some standard differential equations in certain nice domains, like Laplace equation in a unit disk, by using the Fourier series.
- Students learn how to construct a series of orthonormal polynomial functions by Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process.
- Students learn how to find the Fourier and inverse Fourier transforms, as well as the discrete Fourier transform for a given function.
- Students learn the LU factorization for a given matrix and its relation with Gaussian elimination.
- Students learn how to solve nonlinear systems of equations by Newton's method, and how to solve linear systems of equations by Jacobi, Gauss-Seidal and successive overrelaxation methods, and understand why these methods work or do not work for some linear or nonlinear systems.
- Students learn how to find the eigenvalues of a matrix by QR factorization and understand the mathematics behind.
- Students learn the fast Fourier transform and its applications.
- Students learn how to solve a two-point boundary value problem by a simple finite element method.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Differential Geometry
courses.description:
This course covers basic theory on curves, and surfaces in the Euclidean three space. Topics include: regular curves, Frenet formulas, local theory of curves, global properties of curves such as isoperimetric inequality, regular surfaces, 1st and 2nd fundamental form, Gaussian curvature and mean curvature, Gauss map, special surfaces such as ruled surfaces, surfaces of revolution, minimal surfaces, intrinsic geometry: geodesic, and Gauss-Bonnet Theorem. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in advanced calculus, linear algebra, and elementary differential equations.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken MATH4033.
courses.learning_outcomes:
- Students learn ways to describe curves and surfaces in space, by equations and parametrizations.

- Students learn the differential approach to regular geometric objects, using moving frames and searching for complete local invariants. In particular, they learn the Frenet frame, curvature and torsion of regular space curves.

- Students use integration techniques to study some global theorems on plane curves and methods of ordinary differential equations to obtain curves with prescribed curvature and torsion.

- Students learn the formulation of regular surfaces in 3 dimensions, their orientability, differentiable structure and metric structure.

- Students learn the Gauss map and its many important consequences.

- Students learn computations of various curvatures through examples and special surfaces.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Real Analysis
courses.description:
This is an introductory course on the Lebesgue integration theory on real line. Topics include: measurable sets, measurable functions, Lebesgue integral, Fatou's lemma, monotone convergence theorem, Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem and differentiation. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in elementary analysis.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken any one of IMSC2058, 2068, 2230. Pre-requisite: MATH2050/2058.
courses.learning_outcomes:
- Students learn the basic properties of measurable sets and measurable functions on the real line.

- Students learn the introduction of Lebesgue integration and its basic properties.

- Students learn the fundamental convergence theorems including Fatou's lemma, monotone convergence theorem, Lebesgue dominate convergence theorem and results in connection with differentiation.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Complex Analysis
courses.description:
This course is designed for students who are intending to acquire advanced theoretical understanding about analytic functions, which is typically needed for further studies. The course emphasizes the rigorous treatment of the analysis of complex functions. Students are expected to have sophisticated mathematics background and superb theoretical knowledge in multivariable calculus. Major topics include entire functions of infinite series and infinite products, normal families, theory of conformal mappings. Details are given in course syllabus.

Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students taken who have taken any one of IMSC2018/2028/2058/2068/2230. Pre-requisite: MATH2230 and MATH3060.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students will be able to state and prove important theorems about analytic functions, including sequence or series of functions, local and global theories.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Financial Mathematics
courses.description:
Topics of this course will include: Basic option theory, forward and futures contracts, model of asset price, Ito's Lemma, asset price random walk, Black-Scholes model, free boundary problems of options, constrained matrix problems and the projected SOR method, discrete random walk model and the binomial methods. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in probability and differential equations.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.learning_outcomes:
In this course, the students are expected to learn

- European Options

- American Options

- Interest Rates

- Put-Call Parity

- Trading Strategies

- Geometric Brownian Motions

- Ito's Lemma

- Black-Scholes Equations

- Extension of Black-Scholes Model

- Binomial Method

- Monte Carlo Methods

- Finite Difference Methods

courses.title: Partial Differential Equations

meetings.location: Fung King Hey Bldg Swire Hall1

Fung King Hey Bldg Swire Hall1

courses.description:
This is an introduction to the classical theory of partial differential equations. Topics are usually selected from: First-order equations, types of second-order equations, well-posedness of the wave and the heat equations, boundary value problems for the Laplace and Poisson equations, separation of variables. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in advanced calculus.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.learning_outcomes:
In general, the goal is to let the student understand the basic properties of the three principal types- hyperbolic, elliptic and parabolic equations. After taking and passing this course, a student is expected

- to distinguish the types of the equations and use change of variables to simplify them,

- to solve well-posed problems by the method of separation of variables. (In particular, he/she should be able to use this method to solve the mixed problems including one-dimensional wave and heat equations as well as the boundary value problems for the Laplace equation on a disk.)

- on the theoretical side, to know how the method of separation of variables is related to eigenvalue problems. (Rigorous proofs of convergence of the series of solutions should also be understood.)

- to learn well the solution of the Cauchy problem for the wave equations in low dimensions by the method of spherical means,

- to learn well the solution of the Cauchy problem for the heat equation by the heat kernel or by Fourier transform. The characteristic properties of heat flows and wave motions should be well-understood.

- to know the Poison formula for the solution of the Laplace equation on a ball and have some idea of solving the problem over a general domain by Perron’s method, and

- to understand well various maximum principle as they are applied to the uniqueness issues for elliptic and parabolic equations.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Optimization Theory
courses.description:
Unconstrained and equality optimization models, constrained problems, optimality conditions for constrained extrema, convex sets and functions, duality in nonlinear convex programming, descent methods, conjugate direction methods and quasi-Newton methods. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in advanced calculus.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.

courses.description:
Bernoulli processes and sum of independent random variables, Poisson processes, times of arrivals, Markov chains, transient and recurrent states, stationary distribution of Markov chains, Markov pure jump processes, and birth and death processes. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in probability.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken IERG3300.
courses.learning_outcomes:
This is a second course in probability theory. We expect students to learn systems which vary in time in a random manner. In the course they will learn the use of probability and mathematics in the theory and to see many examples that are related to real life problems. The basic learning outcomes are:

- Students will be familiar with the basic probability notations: independence, conditioning, random variables, distributions, expected values, moments.

- Students learn the important concept of Markov chain, transition probability, hitting time, transient and recurrent states. They will learn the computation techniques in linear analysis, and examples like gambler’s ruin problem, birth and death chains, branching chains, queuing chains.

- Students learn the stationary distribution, existence and uniqueness, convergence and long time behavior, applications to real life problems.

- Students learn the continuous-time Markov chains, basic properties, generator of the chains, differential equation technique, Poisson processes, birth and death processes queuing chains.

- Students learn the Gaussian processes and Brownian motions.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Game Theory
courses.description:
Principles and techniques of game theory, matrix games, minimax theorem and calculation of optimal strategies, cooperative and non-cooperative solutions of bimatrix games, coalitional games and applications. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in linear algebra.
Advisory: MATH Majors should select not more than 5 MATH courses in a term.
courses.learning_outcomes:
We expect the students to understand the mathematics and quantitative techniques behind the game theory. The theory will be illustrated by plenty of examples. Through this students will be exposed to practical problem decision making and in economics including optimization, bargaining, cooperation, coalition and voting strategies. The basic learning outcomes are:

- Students understand the basic step of games: the game tree, games with chances, information set, strategies, payoffs, equilibrium of strategies.

- Students learn the basic mathematics and examples in two person zero-sum games: saddle point, mixed strategy, minimax theorem. They need to sue matrix theory and linear programming to solve the problems.

- Students learn the non-zero sum games which includes cooperative, non-cooperative games, Nash’s equilibrium and Nash’s axiom of bargaining and the mathematics to attack these problems.

- Students learn the N-person cooperative games including strategy for coalition, Shapley value, voting games.

This course focuses on the applications of mathematical data analytic tools in a variety of science, medical, financial and engineering problems. Students will become familiar with mathematical tools and models for essential topics/case-studies selected from, but not limited to, algorithm trading, fraud detection, digital advertising, medical imaging, bioinformatics, remote sensing, and social networks. courses.learning_outcomes:
On completion of this course, students will be able to:
• Analyze, evaluate, interpret, organize and synthesize information in a practical and quantitative manner.
• Understand in-depth the various problems and the technical difficulties in solving them.
• Apply sophisticated modelling and computational techniques to critically examine the problem and solution methods

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Real Analysis I
courses.description:
This course is an introduction to real analysis on abstract spaces. The following contents are covered: Integration on a measure space, the construction of measures from outer measures, Riesz representation theorem relating positive functionals to measures, Lebesque and Hausdorff measures, Lebesgue spaces and their duality, weak convergence of functions, signed measures and Radon-Nikodym theorem.
Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in Lebesgue integration on the real line and elements of functional analysis.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For research postgraduate students under Division of Mathematics. Approval is needed for students in BSc Mathematics, BEd Mathematics and Mathematics Education or BSc Mathematics and Information Engineering.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To understand the modern theory of measure and integration and the functional properties of measurable functions.
2. To familiarize the skills in analysis.
3. To have prepared for written qualifying examinations in the subject of analysis in major research universities.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Theory of Partial Differential Equations I
courses.description: This is course is devoted to introducing fundamental theories on evolution equations. In particular, the course concentrates on the following types of evolution equations: second-order parabolic equations, second-order hyperbolic equations, system of conservations laws and some nonlinear wave equations.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For research postgraduate students under Division of Mathematics, also available to undergraduate students majored in mathematics. Approval is needed for students in MSc Mathematics or MSc Math Education.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Theory of Partial Differential Equations II
courses.description:
This course covers the basic theory of partial differential equations equations with emphasis on elliptic equations of second order. Both the classical and modern approaches to these equations are discussed. The main concern is various a prior estimates which are useful in solving linear and nonlinear equations. Some geometric applications are included. It is suited for those who are interested
in analysis or geometry.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For research postgraduate students under Division of Mathematics. Approval is needed for students in BSc Mathematics, BEd Mathematics and Mathematics Education, BSc Mathematics and Information Engineering, MSc Mathematics or MSc Math Education.
courses.learning_outcomes: The basic elliptic theory enables students to understand research papers involving elliptic equations and geometric analysis as well as equips them with necessary tools to embark on their own research.

courses.title: Abstract Algebra I
courses.description: This course is intended to provide a comprehensive and solid foundation in abstract algebra. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in a first course in algebra.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For research postgraduate students under Division of Mathematics. Approval is needed for students in BSc Mathematics, BEd Mathematics and Mathematics Education or BSc Mathematics and Information Engineering.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To have a basic understanding of general abstract algebra
2. To be ready for graduate studies in algebra-related subjects such as algebraic geometry, number theory, representation theory, etc
3. To be prepared for written qualifying examinations in the area of algebra for major research universities in the world.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Riemannian Geometry I
courses.description: This course is intended to provide a solid background in Riemannian Geometry. Topics include: affine connection, tensor calculus, Riemannian metric, geodesics, curvature tensor, completeness and some global theory. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in differential geometry of curves and surfaces.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For research postgraduate students under Division of Mathematics. Approval is needed for students in BSc Mathematics, BEd Mathematics and Mathematics Education or BSc Mathematics and Information Engineering.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To recognize the definitions and properties of basic objects in Riemannian geometry (including metrics, tensors, geodesics, and curvatures)
2. To develop basic computational skill in Tensor calculus
3. To be ready for further studies related to Riemannian geometry.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Topology of Manifolds
courses.description: This course is an introduction to several basic topological invariants for manifolds. Major topics are: topological and differentiable manifolds, maps between manifolds, Sard's Theorem, degree of maps and vector fields, fundamental group, covering space, simplices and homology group, differential forms and cohomology group. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge in elementary analysis and basic topology and algebra.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For research postgraduate students under Division of Mathematics. Approval is needed for students in BSc Mathematics, BEd Mathematics and Mathematics Education or BSc Mathematics and Information Engineering.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To recognize the definitions and properties of several basic topological invariants for manifolds.
2. To be ready for further studies related to manifolds (smooth, Riemannian, or complex).
3. To have prepared for written qualifying examinations in the area of topology for major research universities in the world.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Advanced Numerical Analysis II
courses.description: This course covers basic numerical methods in the graduate level. The main themes are numerical solutions of PDEs and numerical methods for eigenvalue problems. For numerical solutions of PDEs, some basic theories of finite difference methods for hyperbolic equations are discussed. The topics include stability, order of accuracy, consistency, Lax-equivalence theorem, multistep methods, dissipation and dispersion, system of equations in higher dimensions, splitting schemes. For numerical methods for eigenvalue problems, the topics include the Gershgorin theorem, power iteration, inverse power iteration, Householder and Givens matrices, QR factorization, QR algorithm, singular value decomposition, principle component analysis, rank deficient problems, regularization techniques.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For MPhil-PhD Mathematics. Approval is needed for students in BSc Mathematics, BEd Mathematics and Mathematics Education or BSc Mathematics and Information Engineering.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Students are expected to learn the basic theories of finite difference method for PDE as well as some classical iterative methods for linear algebraic and eigenvalue problems. The learning outcomes are
- Students learn how to construct finite difference schemes for hyperbolic PDE.
- Students learn how to analyze the stability by the Fourier method.
- Students learn how to prove convergence and consistency.
- Students learn how to construct multistep methods.
- Students learn how to analyze dissipation and dispersion.
- Students learn how to construct and analyze schemes for hyperbolic systems in multi-dimensions.
- Students learn how to construct and analyze splitting schemes.
- Students learn some basic iterative method for eigenvalue problems, including power and inverse power iteration, as well as QR algorithm.
- Students learn how to compute the Householder and Givens matrices, QR factorization and singular value decomposition, together with their applications.
- Students learn the theory and applications of principle component analysis.
- Students learn how to solve rank deficient problems and their regularization techniques..
